newsitem.title: USA: NBC head looks askance at free political air time.
newsitem.headline: NBC head looks askance at free political air time.

text.p: NBC President Robert Wright Tuesday rejected a proposal that local television stations give some nonpresidential candidates free air time, saying nightly five-minute campaign talks would be boring.

"Everything in our bones tells us that vignettes by politicians -- that's not an attractive programming concept," Wright said after an appearance at an industry conference sponsored by Broadcasting & Cable magazine.
Wright said political candidates received extensive coverage on news programs produced by NBC, a unit of General Electric Co.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt had proposed that television companies operating local stations give free air time to candidates for the Senate, the House and state governorships. He said he would work to win wide industry agreement on the proposal after the presidential election.

A. H. Belo Corp., a newspaper and televison company based in Texas, has agreed to give five-minute slots to Senate, House and gubernatorial candidates on its seven stations, Hundt said. The giveaway to the nonpresidential candidates was the first by a commerical station in the United States, an aide to Hundt said.

Hundt told reporters after a speech at the conference that he aimed to spur industry discussion of his proposal and did not believe regulations would be required to obtain wide adoption of the idea by the roughly 1,500 local television stations across the United States.

Peter Lund, chief executive of CBS Inc., the television network owned by Westinghouse Electric, said scheduling the scores of nonpresidential candidates in many televison markets would be a logistical nightmare. Any changes in using television for elections should be part of overall campaign reform, he said.
Lund said he knew of no evidence that suggested giving free air time to candidates would cut back paid political advertising.

Political advertising is a major profit source for U.S. broadcasters, giving lifts to industry earnings, especially during presidental elections every four years. An extended debate was touched off earlier this year by an offer of free time for presidential candidates from the Fox network, owned by News Corp. Ltd
